# Repository secret scanning

This policy gives repository maintainers and automation authors one durable contract for leak prevention. It governs committed configuration, local hooks, hosted CI, scanner output, and exceptions across every bundle.

Primary sources are the repository's `AGENTS.md`, `SPEC.md`, scanner and task configuration, the operator's 2026-07-20 approval of this design, and the official Infisical documentation for [secret scanning](https://infisical.com/docs/cli/scanning-overview), [scan commands](https://infisical.com/docs/cli/commands/scan), [Git change scanning](https://infisical.com/docs/cli/commands/scan-git-changes), and [project configuration](https://infisical.com/docs/cli/project-config).

Secret-class ownership and repository storage boundaries are defined in [secrets ownership and repository boundaries](secrets-policy.md); this document governs scanner behavior and enforcement scopes.

## Current allocation

The operator approved GitGuardian as the sole hosted PR secret scanner,
retaining Infisical for local checks and explicit audits. The
[GitGuardian record](gitguardian-scanning.md) preserves settings and evidence
limits. Direct-to-main with selective PR review remains intentional; mandatory
merge enforcement is deferred.

The repository task graph implements this allocation: `ci` is shared validation
and `check:local` adds current-file scanning. Hosted validation and GitGuardian
results must still be checked for each published PR head.

## Local hook installation and reinstallation

The initial 2026-09-05 inspection found the declared pre-commit hook absent.
A separately authorized installation later that day connected hk 1.57.0 to
Git on Apple Git 2.50.1 while preserving Entire 0.10.5 chaining. Main and all
linked worktrees share this clone's hooks directory; this does not establish
installation in other clones or on other machines.

The installed composition is `pre-commit` invoking hk through mise, and
`commit-msg` invoking Entire before executable `commit-msg.pre-entire` invokes
hk. Other Entire Git lifecycle hooks were preserved. Both hk shims disable
mise automatic dependency installation. Disposable runtime checks rejected
merge markers and an invalid conventional message, accepted a valid commit,
and traced Entire-to-hk chaining. The staged scan used system Infisical
0.43.121; it did not verify the old main pin 0.43.128 or transcript capture.

**Reinstallation caveat:** an unqualified `hk install` can overwrite the
composed `commit-msg` hook on this observed toolchain. Before reinstalling,
inspect the effective hook directory and `core.hooksPath`, back up existing
hooks, and prepare the hk scripts in an isolated repository. Preserve Entire's
entry point and its `.pre-entire` chain to hk, together with the automatic-
installation guards. Validate rejection and acceptance with disposable
commits and trace the chain before replacing shared hooks. Recheck every
linked worktree afterward. Do not assume a future installer preserves this
composition without verification.

Source: the authorized installation receipt and subsequent installed-script
hash verification on 2026-09-05. Clone-local receipts, saved scripts, hashes,
and guarded rollback live under
`.git/hook-backups/20260905-hk-1.57.0/` in the common Git directory; these are
not tracked or portable recovery artifacts. Locate that directory with
`git rev-parse --git-common-dir`. Recheck hook presence in fresh clones; when
absent, run `mise run secrets:staged` explicitly before committing.

## Identifier and configuration policy

Never commit credentials, device serial numbers, hardware UUIDs, or unredacted identifiers that materially expose a person, account, credential, or device. Syntax alone does not determine sensitivity: a UUID-shaped value can be a sensitive hardware identifier, or it can be a non-secret service linkage identifier.

Reviewed project or workspace identifiers may be committed only when the identifier grants no access and its containing file holds no credentials. On that basis, the repository tracks `.infisical.json`: it links CLI operations to an Infisical workspace but does not contain an access token or secret value. Any future schema or content change requires another review before commit.

All three scanner configurations extend Infisical's default rules. `.infisical-scan.toml` is the shared Git-facing configuration for staged, bounded-range, and full-history scans; `.infisical-current-files-scan.toml` governs only the current-files scan; and `.infisical-transcripts-scan.toml` governs only the explicit transcript audit. None adds a generic UUID detector because such a rule would conflate identifier shape with sensitivity and would flag the approved project linkage configuration. A future custom rule must target evidence of a secret or sensitive identifier class, not a broad syntax shared by benign values, and scanner-rule changes must review all three configurations.

The current-files-only configuration excludes only `.entire/metadata/`. Entire metadata is gitignored, machine-local session state that varies independently of the checked-out repository and is absent from a normal hosted checkout. This is a scan-scope boundary rather than a detector exception. The shared Git-facing configuration has no path allowlist, so staged, bounded-range, and full-history scans still detect force-added or historical Entire metadata. The transcript configuration has no path allowlist, and `mise run secrets:transcripts` must not be treated as evidence that metadata is safe merely because it is outside repository CI.

## Enforcement scopes

| Scope | Command | When it runs | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hosted PR commits | `GitGuardian Security Checks` | GitGuardian GitHub App | Scan PR commits independently of Actions; reports failures without mandatory merge enforcement. |
| Staged changes | `mise run secrets:staged` | Installed hk pre-commit check in the verified local clone; explicit invocation where absent | Block a leak before a commit is created. |
| Current repository files | `mise run secrets:files` | Local `mise run check:local` | Cover the checked-out tree except reproducible upstream materializations and machine-local Entire metadata. |
| Local Entire transcripts | `mise run secrets:transcripts` | Explicit local audit | Scan gitignored `.entire/metadata/` independently of repository CI; findings remain blocking for claims about transcript cleanliness but do not classify tracked repository changes. |
| Bounded commit range | `mise run secrets:range` | Explicit local audit | Inspect newly introduced Git history without rescanning the established history baseline. |
| Full history | `mise run secrets:history` | Explicit local audit | Establish or recheck the baseline after adoption, rule changes, suspected exposure, or an audit request. |

GitGuardian's GitHub App runs PR scanning independently of GitHub Actions.
The hosted workflow runs `mise run ci` for PRs, main pushes, tags, and manual
dispatch; it does not invoke Infisical. Direct-push GitGuardian coverage and
full-history scope have not been independently verified. Local Infisical is
resolved from the installed executable on PATH; this repository no longer pins
it through mise or claims shared scanner-version parity with hosted execution.
The shared validation tasks still have identical local/hosted pass semantics.

## Output, reports, and exceptions

All committed tasks request redacted output, disable telemetry, and avoid creating a report file by default. A normal successful or failed gate should remain console output, not durable registry content. Scanner reports can retain sensitive filenames, line locations, rule names, and finding context even when secret values are redacted; stale reports also look authoritative after the tree changes. Generate a report only for a specific diagnostic or review need, place it in a temporary or explicitly approved artifact location, inspect it before sharing, and remove it when that need ends.

Do not add a blanket report path to `.gitignore` before a real workflow defines that path and its lifecycle. Do not add an allow rule or baseline entry merely to make a gate pass. An exception must identify the exact detector and narrow match, explain why the value is not a secret, name the owning concept or configuration, and be followed by a full-history scan when it changes detector behavior. No committed scanner baseline is required while the repository is clean under the configured rules.

Infisical supplies local secret checks; GitGuardian supplies hosted PR checks. Bumblebee supplies secondary endpoint package inventory and exact-version exposure-catalog matching; see its [installation and usage record](../mac-studio/tools/bumblebee.md). It remains outside blocking repository gates. fnox and the broader missing-mise-version inventory are deferred toolchain work and are not part of this scanning policy.

# Decision Log

## 2026-07-20 — adopt scoped Infisical enforcement

The operator approved committing `.infisical.json`, rejected a blanket UUID detector, and chose Infisical's default detector set. Local pre-commit enforcement covers staged changes; ordinary hosted CI covers current files and introduced commits; full history is an explicit baseline or audit operation rather than a cost paid on every clean run.

Generated scan reports are not ignored preemptively. This preserves an intentional review boundary if a report workflow is later introduced and avoids normalizing sensitive or stale scanner output as a repository byproduct.

## 2026-07-21 — separate repository CI from local transcript auditing

After the deleted synthetic canary repeatedly blocked unrelated repository changes through gitignored Entire metadata, the operator approved a separate scan boundary. `mise run secrets:files` excludes `.entire/metadata/` so repository CI reflects checked-out project content, while `mise run secrets:transcripts` retains explicit redacted coverage of the local session corpus. This is a routing decision, not a detector exception or an assertion that transcripts are safe. No transcript content, finding baseline, fingerprint allow rule, staged enforcement, bounded history scan, or full-history behavior changed.

## 2026-07-21 — link scanner enforcement to secret ownership policy

Keep scanning mechanics in this Policy and link the separate ownership Policy so neither document implies access to Infisical, 1Password, or live secret state.

## 2026-08-15 — let executable configuration own the scanner version

After automated dependency updates advanced Infisical from the version named
in this Policy to `0.43.121`, stop duplicating the exact pin in current Policy
prose. `mise.toml` is the empirical source for the reviewed executable version;
this Policy continues to own why local and hosted enforcement share that pin.
Historical Incident, design, and plan records retain the versions that were
true at their own observation boundaries.

## 2026-09-04 — approve distinct hosted and local scanning responsibilities

The prior policy assigned Infisical to both local and hosted enforcement. The
operator identified duplicate hosted coverage; inspection confirmed GitGuardian
scanned all six PR #19 commits and is configured to return Failed on detection.
Approve GitGuardian as the sole hosted PR scanner, retaining local Infisical
pre-commit checks and explicit audits. This does not claim identical detectors
or verified full-history coverage. Executable migration remains pending.

GitHub merge enforcement remains an open, separate decision: `main` had no
protection or effective rulesets at inspection. The
[GitGuardian record](gitguardian-scanning.md) owns the observed configuration
and resolution/verification procedure. No branch rules were changed.

## 2026-09-05 — defer mandatory merge enforcement

The operator resolved the earlier open question by retaining direct-to-main
and selecting PRs according to risk and review need. PR #19 retains its review
path; its merge is not approved by this decision. Required checks and mandatory
PRs are deferred to preserve registry pacing. Revisit on repeated breakage,
missed meaningful review, or coordination failures that selective PRs do not
contain. Existing local validation and publication approvals still apply.

## 2026-09-05 — implement separate hosted and local scan gates

Remove hosted Infisical range/history commands and its transitive dependency
from `ci`. Add `check:local` to compose shared CI with current-file scanning;
retain staged, range, history, and transcript audit commands. Regression tests
exercise the public mise dry-run plans and hosted workflow boundary. Record the
missing installed pre-commit hook and require explicit staged scanning until
that separate installation gap is repaired. Earlier pending-migration entries
remain historical rationale. Hosted run results belong to their exact PR head.


## 2026-09-05 — record installed hooks and reinstall boundary

Supersede the earlier missing-hook observation with the separate installation
receipt. Record verified shared-clone enforcement, Entire chaining, scanner
version limits, and the overwrite risk from unqualified hk reinstallation.
Preserve explicit staged scanning as the fallback for unverified fresh clones.

## 2026-10-02 — remove upstream path exclusions

The operator retired the `upstream/` provenance lock and vendored payloads.
Remove the `upstream/src/` and `upstream/docs/` allowlist paths from both
`.infisical-scan.toml` and `.infisical-current-files-scan.toml`, and their
`.gitignore` entries, so no scan scope excludes a path that no longer exists.
The Entire metadata exclusion is unchanged. This narrows scan exclusions.

{"body":"## Summary

This branch applies the governance draft from #29. It researches how to enforce the boundary between research and knowledge, makes the first promotion pass into governance, and restructures AGENTS.md around the repository's layers. Commits were kept to one layer at a time where possible, which the branch now asks for.

## What changed

**Research** (`research/`, all `status: draft`):

- OKF plugin scope: OpenKnowledge treats the whole repository as one bundle and has no path scoping.
- OpenWiki: evidence-versioned claims, source trust by kind, and tool-owned write boundaries.
- A write-boundary brief and two passes:
  - BB is ruled out as the enforcement point, because no permission mode gates file writes by path.
  - Repository-held enforcement works at commit time, through diff structure.
- OpenWiki commit history: 12 of 419 commits mix its tool and its generated wiki, held low by a path-restricted bot. The same measure here finds 12 of 145.
- A research brief for a repository-held maintaining tool (`src/`), with the compiler-trap risk recorded as standing backpressure.

**Governance (first promotion pass, knowledge-only commit):**

- Enforcement is held by the repository.
- Layer separation is tolerated and measured as a signal, not a gate.
- Knowledge gets a sanctioned writer limited by a path list, run locally first and on a CI schedule once reliable.
- OpenKnowledge is rejected for this repository.
- The Decision Log ratifies one earlier layer-mixing edit.

**Knowledge:** new `tools/qmd.md` and `resources/mothership-vault.md` for the Mac Studio, moved out of AGENTS.md.

**Sources:** an observation that the research layer held the boundary only through operator attention, and a session knowledge capture.

**Machinery:**

- AGENTS.md is restructured around repository boundaries, governing documents stated by condition, and a change protocol. It is about 76 lines, down from 134.
- A stale hook-gap line is fixed.
- The `session-knowledge-capture` skill is added with its Claude symlink.

## Known open items

These are recorded in governance and the research documents:

- the design of the maintaining tool (agent brief questions 1 to 7);
- how to commit a tool change that forces a content migration;
- the standard for the mixing rate;
- the device-incident skills backlog;
- retiring OpenKnowledge after this session, including replacing its index generation.

## Validation

`mise run check:local` passes on every commit, covering OKF validation and fixtures, agent-integration, CI-boundary and skill tests, and local current-file secret scanning.

---
type: Policy
title: Shared Epistemic Contract
description: Canonical human-and-agent authority contract for intent, evidence, uncertainty, ontology, and change over time.
status: stable
tags: [ repo, governance, epistemics, human-agent ]
---

# Shared Epistemic Contract

This Policy is the canonical shared contract for humans and agents working in
this repository. It governs how repository specifications and architectures
relate to operator intent, empirical evidence, uncertainty, and later
disagreement. Audience-specific entry points may explain why this contract
matters, but they must link here rather than restate it as competing truth.

The approved authority and ownership rationale is preserved in the
[Shared Epistemic Contract Authority Design](../../docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-10-shared-epistemic-contract-authority-design.md).

# Authority Boundary

The user is ground truth for goals, meanings, preferences, and operating
decisions. The architecture serves that intent; it must not reinterpret the
user merely to preserve its own consistency.

Observable machine state and primary sources remain ground truth for empirical
claims about the machine or an external system. User intent does not make an
empirical claim true, and an observed fact does not decide what the user should
value. When intent, recorded claims, and empirical evidence disagree, preserve
and expose the disagreement rather than silently privileging the current
architecture.

# Shared Principles

## The user is ground truth, not the architecture

Repository structure, specifications, validators, and tools are instruments
for the user's intent. They do not acquire independent authority to overrule
that intent. The evidence boundary above remains part of this principle.

## The system is correct for the user, not universally correct

This is an operator-specific working system. Upstream formats, tools, and
conventions are useful when they solve an observed personal-computing problem;
they are not automatic conformance targets whose abstractions outrank local
use. Local success does not establish universal correctness.

## Future disagreement must be auditable

Future-me must be able to disagree with past-me and identify where divergence
began. A material change must preserve the previous position, the observation
or decision that challenged it, the newly operative position, and when the
change became effective. Git shows that text changed; durable rationale must
make why it changed discoverable.

## Ontology must emerge from usage

A new concept, field, relationship, or lifecycle begins as a hypothesis. It may
remain ordinary prose and links while usage is sparse. Repeated use across real
records is evidence that a shared convention may be useful. Only demonstrated
stability and utility justify hard validator enforcement. Do not finalize an
ontology merely to make an early architecture internally complete.

## Never force premature closure

Uncertainty, disagreement, partial observations, unresolved links, and
competing hypotheses are valid states. Intake and validation must not require a
final classification, cause, or resolution when the evidence does not support
one. Closure is an observed outcome with evidence, not a formatting
requirement.

## Link observations into trajectories over time

Preserve events as events instead of continually rewriting them into one
timeless claim. Link observations, recurrences, hypotheses, decisions,
interventions, and later outcomes so humans and agents can follow change over
time. Begin with prose and existing links. Let repeated usage determine whether
additional fields or validator rules are warranted.

# Contract Operation

## One contract for both audiences

Humans and agents consume this same canonical interpretation. `README.md` is a
human orientation surface, `AGENTS.md` is an agent operating surface, and
`SPEC.md` is the presently operative technical contract. None of them owns a
separate version of these principles.

## Current state and historical rationale

Current state may be rewritten. Historical rationale must be superseded, not
erased.

This Policy presents the current interpretation cleanly rather than collecting
contradictory versions in its main prose. When a material principle or
interpretation changes, append a Decision Log entry that identifies the prior
position, challenging evidence, replacement decision, and effective date. A
superseding record must identify what it replaces, and older rationale must
remain discoverable as history rather than masquerading as current authority.

## Specification and validation

`SPEC.md` remains the currently operative, revisable technical contract. This
Policy governs how that specification is interpreted and changed; it does not
silently invalidate existing rules. Technical changes still require a
deliberate decision and proportionate validation.

Do not promote a new architectural or ontological hypothesis into hard
validation merely because it can be expressed as a rule. First collect usage
evidence, preserve disagreement, and determine whether the proposed constraint
is a durable invariant, a revisable convention, or an unsupported hypothesis.

## Path and architecture migration

The current `_repo` location is an implementation decision, not an eternal
principle. This contract's semantic authority belongs to its explicitly
designated canonical successor and survives a future path, bundle, or broader
architecture migration.

A migration must update the human, agent, specification, and registry pointers
in the same bounded change; record the previous and new locations and the
reason for moving; and preserve a discoverable link from earlier decision
history to the successor. Moving the contract does not authorize changing its
principles. When location and substance both change, preserve distinct
rationale for each decision.

# Decision Log

## 2026-08-10 — adopt one shared human-and-agent contract

Adopt this `_repo` Policy as the canonical contract for both audiences. Keep
operator intent, empirical evidence, and architectural interpretation as
distinct authority surfaces; make specifications revisable; allow ontology to
emerge from usage; preserve uncertainty; and connect observations over time.

This decision implements the approved dated design and contains the mechanism
recorded in [VIO-0002](../../sources/vio/vio-0002-premature-architectural-closure.md). It does not
resolve that Violation or invalidate current technical rules.
---
type: Policy
title: Agent capability and Python development contract
description: Policy for composing repo-owned agent guidance, activating work-specific capabilities, and governing executable Python structure and validation.
tags: [ agents, contracts, python, tdd, validation ]
timestamp: 2026-08-06T00:00:00Z
status: stable
aliases: [ development contract, agent capability contract, Python contract ]
---

# Agent capability and Python development contract

## Capability activation

Capabilities apply according to the work being performed. Investigation and evidence gathering use the research discipline. Durable registry prose uses the writing discipline. Plans and migrations use the planning discipline. Executable implementation and tooling changes use the coding and TDD discipline. Python changes also use the Python discipline. Validation scripts, hooks, CI, and generators additionally use the automation and local-to-hosted parity discipline.

This activation model preserves the repository's research, writing, planning, and coding functions without making every rule govern every edit. A prose-only registry correction does not require a RED test. A Python validator change does.

## Python and validation policy

Executable Python changes use RED, GREEN, and REFACTOR. Existing behavior must first be characterized through public interfaces. Refactoring must preserve observable behavior, diagnostic codes, ordering, CLI exit semantics, and documented import surfaces unless an approved design explicitly changes them.

Run Python through `uv`. Standalone reusable scripts use PEP 723 metadata and Google-style docstrings. The canonical repository CI gate must include every deterministic test and validation task that is required for completion; a green umbrella task is not sufficient when a required focused suite can still fail independently.

Production and test files are limited to 200 lines, constructs to 30 lines, and nesting depth to three. These limits are hard by default. They are intended to expose mixed responsibilities and hidden control-flow complexity, not to reward compressed code or arbitrary file proliferation.

## Structural exceptions

A structural exception requires explicit operator approval before merge and must be recorded in this policy's active-exceptions section. Each entry must identify the exact file or construct, measured limit, reason normal decomposition would reduce clarity or duplicate a boundary, alternatives considered, smallest approved scope, validation evidence, owner, and removal condition. Deadlines, convenience, legacy size, and avoidance of test changes are not sufficient rationales. An exception may not authorize unrelated growth, and later work touching the exception must preserve or reduce its scope.

### Active exceptions

None.

# Shared Epistemic Contract

This Policy is the canonical shared contract for humans and agents working in
this repository. It governs how repository specifications and architectures
relate to operator intent, empirical evidence, uncertainty, and later
disagreement. Audience-specific entry points may explain why this contract
matters, but they must link here rather than restate it as competing truth.

The approved authority and ownership rationale is preserved in the
[Shared Epistemic Contract Authority Design](../../docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-10-shared-epistemic-contract-authority-design.md).

# Authority Boundary

The user is ground truth for goals, meanings, preferences, and operating
decisions. The architecture serves that intent; it must not reinterpret the
user merely to preserve its own consistency.

Observable machine state and primary sources remain ground truth for empirical
claims about the machine or an external system. User intent does not make an
empirical claim true, and an observed fact does not decide what the user should
value. When intent, recorded claims, and empirical evidence disagree, preserve
and expose the disagreement rather than silently privileging the current
architecture.

# Shared Principles

## The user is ground truth, not the architecture

Repository structure, specifications, validators, and tools are instruments
for the user's intent. They do not acquire independent authority to overrule
that intent. The evidence boundary above remains part of this principle.

## The system is correct for the user, not universally correct

This is an operator-specific working system. Upstream formats, tools, and
conventions are useful when they solve an observed personal-computing problem;
they are not automatic conformance targets whose abstractions outrank local
use. Local success does not establish universal correctness.

## Future disagreement must be auditable

Future-me must be able to disagree with past-me and identify where divergence
began. A material change must preserve the previous position, the observation
or decision that challenged it, the newly operative position, and when the
change became effective. Git shows that text changed; durable rationale must
make why it changed discoverable.

## Ontology must emerge from usage

A new concept, field, relationship, or lifecycle begins as a hypothesis. It may
remain ordinary prose and links while usage is sparse. Repeated use across real
records is evidence that a shared convention may be useful. Only demonstrated
stability and utility justify hard validator enforcement. Do not finalize an
ontology merely to make an early architecture internally complete.

## Never force premature closure

Uncertainty, disagreement, partial observations, unresolved links, and
competing hypotheses are valid states. Intake and validation must not require a
final classification, cause, or resolution when the evidence does not support
one. Closure is an observed outcome with evidence, not a formatting
requirement.

## Link observations into trajectories over time

Preserve events as events instead of continually rewriting them into one
timeless claim. Link observations, recurrences, hypotheses, decisions,
interventions, and later outcomes so humans and agents can follow change over
time. Begin with prose and existing links. Let repeated usage determine whether
additional fields or validator rules are warranted.

# Contract Operation

## One contract for both audiences

Humans and agents consume this same canonical interpretation. `README.md` is a
human orientation surface, `AGENTS.md` is an agent operating surface, and
`SPEC.md` is the presently operative technical contract. None of them owns a
separate version of these principles.

## Current state and historical rationale

Current state may be rewritten. Historical rationale must be superseded, not
erased.

This Policy presents the current interpretation cleanly rather than collecting
contradictory versions in its main prose. When a material principle or
interpretation changes, append a Decision Log entry that identifies the prior
position, challenging evidence, replacement decision, and effective date. A
superseding record must identify what it replaces, and older rationale must
remain discoverable as history rather than masquerading as current authority.

## Specification and validation

`SPEC.md` remains the currently operative, revisable technical contract. This
Policy governs how that specification is interpreted and changed; it does not
silently invalidate existing rules. Technical changes still require a
deliberate decision and proportionate validation.

Do not promote a new architectural or ontological hypothesis into hard
validation merely because it can be expressed as a rule. First collect usage
evidence, preserve disagreement, and determine whether the proposed constraint
is a durable invariant, a revisable convention, or an unsupported hypothesis.

## Path and architecture migration

The current `_repo` location is an implementation decision, not an eternal
principle. This contract's semantic authority belongs to its explicitly
designated canonical successor and survives a future path, bundle, or broader
architecture migration.

A migration must update the human, agent, specification, and registry pointers
in the same bounded change; record the previous and new locations and the
reason for moving; and preserve a discoverable link from earlier decision
history to the successor. Moving the contract does not authorize changing its
principles. When location and substance both change, preserve distinct
rationale for each decision.

# Decision Log

## 2026-08-10 — adopt one shared human-and-agent contract

Adopt this `_repo` Policy as the canonical contract for both audiences. Keep
operator intent, empirical evidence, and architectural interpretation as
distinct authority surfaces; make specifications revisable; allow ontology to
emerge from usage; preserve uncertainty; and connect observations over time.

This decision implements the approved dated design and contains the mechanism
recorded in [VIO-0002](../../sources/vio/vio-0002-premature-architectural-closure.md). It does not
resolve that Violation or invalidate current technical rules.

# Agent capability and Python development contract

## Capability activation

Capabilities apply according to the work being performed. Investigation and evidence gathering use the research discipline. Durable registry prose uses the writing discipline. Plans and migrations use the planning discipline. Executable implementation and tooling changes use the coding and TDD discipline. Python changes also use the Python discipline. Validation scripts, hooks, CI, and generators additionally use the automation and local-to-hosted parity discipline.

This activation model preserves the repository's research, writing, planning, and coding functions without making every rule govern every edit. A prose-only registry correction does not require a RED test. A Python validator change does.

## Python and validation policy

Executable Python changes use RED, GREEN, and REFACTOR. Existing behavior must first be characterized through public interfaces. Refactoring must preserve observable behavior, diagnostic codes, ordering, CLI exit semantics, and documented import surfaces unless an approved design explicitly changes them.

Run Python through `uv`. Standalone reusable scripts use PEP 723 metadata and Google-style docstrings. The canonical repository CI gate must include every deterministic test and validation task that is required for completion; a green umbrella task is not sufficient when a required focused suite can still fail independently.

Production and test files are limited to 200 lines, constructs to 30 lines, and nesting depth to three. These limits are hard by default. They are intended to expose mixed responsibilities and hidden control-flow complexity, not to reward compressed code or arbitrary file proliferation.

## Structural exceptions

A structural exception requires explicit operator approval before merge and must be recorded in this policy's active-exceptions section. Each entry must identify the exact file or construct, measured limit, reason normal decomposition would reduce clarity or duplicate a boundary, alternatives considered, smallest approved scope, validation evidence, owner, and removal condition. Deadlines, convenience, legacy size, and avoidance of test changes are not sufficient rationales. An exception may not authorize unrelated growth, and later work touching the exception must preserve or reduce its scope.

### Active exceptions

None.

# Observation Log: The Research Layer Held the Boundary

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Project | personal-computing (3I lab) |
| Captured | 2026-10-05 |
| Observation period | 2026-10-04 late evening through 2026-10-05 early morning |
| Subject | First use of the sources / research / knowledge split on governance work |
| Record type | Operator observation and preliminary assessment, drafted by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) from the operator's statements and the session record |
| Status | Captured while fresh; not yet validated |

## Important disclaimer

This record captures what I noticed right after two research passes on branch `feat/governance-application`. An agent drafted it from my statements and from what happened in the session; I have not reviewed it line by line. It rests on one session and one sequence of events. It is not a finding that the split works in general, and it is not an assessment of the agent.

## Positive observations

What naturally fell out: we created the governance draft, almost kept writing to it, then backed off and wrote research based on the reference examples instead. Five questions fell out as friction. To me that means the split works.

Each kind of material landed in its own layer. The three reference implementations (the OKF reference agent, OpenKnowledge, and OpenWiki) became cited sources. The synthesis became two draft research documents, [OKF plugin scope](../../research/2026-10-04-okf-plugin-scope-and-source-status.md) and [OpenWiki claims and source trust](../../research/2026-10-05-openwiki-claims-and-source-trust.md), each ending in promotion candidates with none applied. The friction became five open questions. The [governance draft](../../bundles/_repo/governance.md) stayed unchanged because nothing had been decided.

The research passes cite each other through their sources rather than through governance, so the evidence chain exists without touching knowledge.

## Open questions

- Would the boundary have held without me redirecting it?
- Do the five questions read differently because they arrived as research friction rather than as edits to governance?
- Is one session enough to say the split works, or only that it can work?

## Negative or surprising observation

The boundary held because I held it, not because anything enforced it. The agent reached for the governance draft twice: first to answer the OKF plugin scoping question directly in its open points, then to add a pointer from governance to the new research. Both times I redirected it, the first time by saying this was a research pass. Nothing in the repository would have refused either edit.

## Experienced pattern

1. The governance draft existed and had open points.
2. A reference implementation answered one of those open points.
3. The agent proposed writing the answer into governance.
4. Inflection point: I named it a research pass, not a governance change.
5. Findings went to `research/` as a draft with promotion candidates; governance stayed unchanged.
6. The same move repeated with OpenWiki, and five open questions fell out of the two passes as friction.

## Impact

The governance draft remains a record of decided things only. The undecided material is collected in two research documents and five questions that can be taken up one at a time, rather than being settled implicitly by the last edit. My attention was needed twice to keep it that way.

## Preliminary assessment

Working hypotheses, plausible and not mutually exclusive:

- **The split works when it is named.** Calling the work a research pass was enough to route it correctly; having `research/` as a real place to put it made the redirection cheap.
- **The boundary depends on operator attention.** The agent's default was to write where the open point lived. Without a refusal mechanism, the boundary is as strong as the operator's vigilance in the moment. This matches the write-boundary finding in the OpenWiki research, where tooling, not the agent, owns what may be written.

## Gap highlighted

- What would make a write to `bundles/` from a research activity refuse or warn without relying on the operator?
- How should an agent recognize that an answer to an open governance point is research, not a governance edit?
- Is "which writes a promotion pass should be refused" the first of the five questions to take up, given this record?

These are questions for later review, not conclusions.

## Next review, if pursued

Compare this record against the two research documents, the unchanged governance draft, the commit history of `feat/governance-application`, and the session in which both redirections happened. Preserve the distinction between what happened, what I concluded about the split, and what the agent's behavior shows about default write targets.

# Repository-held enforcement of the knowledge write boundary

## Purpose and standing

This is Pass 2 of the [write-boundary research brief](2026-10-05-write-boundary-enforcement-brief.md), scoped by [Pass 1](2026-10-05-bb-write-boundary-pass.md), which ruled out BB as the enforcement point and concluded that the repository must carry the guarantee.[^brief][^bb-pass] The question here is how early and how precisely repository-held code can enforce the boundary. It is provisional research; nothing here changes the validator, hooks, or governance.

## Correction to the brief

The brief stated that the pre-commit hook was not installed. That repeated an outdated gap. The scanning policy records that the hook was installed on 2026-09-05 for this clone, chaining Entire to hk, while installation in other clones or on other machines is not established.[^scanning] The installed `pre-commit` hook runs `hk run pre-commit` through mise, and the hook ran on every commit in this session.[^hooks] It runs whitespace, newline, merge-conflict, private-key, and staged-secret checks; it does not run the OKF validator.[^hk]

## Findings

### Q5. Which checks are deterministic from content, and which would have caught the near-misses

The [observation](../sources/observations/2026-10-05-research-layer-held-the-boundary-observation-log.md) records two near-misses: answering the OKF plugin scoping question directly in the governance draft's open points, and adding a pointer from governance to new research.[^observation] Both are edits to a `draft` Policy that already carries `sources`.

Content-only checks read one file state at a time. Candidates include: every bundle concept carries `sources`; a `stable` concept carries a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor; a `draft` concept cites something in `sources/` or `research/`. The governance draft satisfies all of them before and after either near-miss. **No content-only check would have caught either near-miss**, because the problem was not the resulting state but the act of changing knowledge without a promotion.

Diff checks compare a change against its base, and several are deterministic:

- **Separation of layers within a commit.** A single commit may not change both `research/` (or `sources/`) and `bundles/`. Research and promotion become separate units. Both near-misses arose mid-research, so they would most likely have been committed alongside the research they came from (an inference; neither was written). In that case this rule catches both without trusting anything the agent says.
- **Augmentation guards.** Adapted from the OKF reference agent's write guards: an existing bundle concept may not lose `sources` entries or top-level headings.[^ref-agent] These protect against destructive rewrites; they would not catch either near-miss, which only added text.
- **Status transitions.** A concept moving to `stable` must add a new `verified` entry in the same change.

### Q6. How close to write time repository-held code can act

Repository code cannot see a write as it happens; Pass 1 showed no harness-agnostic write-time gate exists.[^bb-pass] The earliest repository-held point every harness and every manual edit reaches is the commit, through the installed pre-commit hook. Adding a validator step there runs the boundary checks for all four harnesses at once. Two limits apply: hooks are clone-local and can be skipped with `--no-verify`. Hosted CI runs `mise run ci` on pull requests and pushes to `main`, but that task does not currently run any of these candidate diff checks. CI could check the same diff only after that validator is wired into the shared task graph. For layer separation, governance has since chosen reporting violations without blocking work; neither hook nor CI would make that signal a rejecting gate.[^ci][^governance]

The commit is also the unit of review in this repository, so enforcement there matches how work is accepted. In both near-misses the proposed change had not yet been written, so nothing at any layer would have fired; the operator's redirection happened at proposal time, which no tool reaches.

### Q7. Telling a promotion from an ordinary edit without trusting the agent

Some structure is visible without self-report: which layers a commit touches, whether `sources` or headings shrank, whether a status moved. Intent is not. Any marker that says "this is a promotion" or "this is maintenance", such as a commit trailer, is written by whoever commits, agent or human. Likewise, a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor proves only that someone wrote one; the repository cannot authenticate that a person verified anything. The structural rules above avoid this by constraining shape rather than reading intent.

### Q8. Cost to legitimate work

The layer-separation rule costs one extra commit per promotion: research lands first, the promotion lands separately and cites it. That matches the governance draft's model, in which a promotion pass is a deliberate step after research.[^governance] Its real cost is mechanical maintenance that crosses layers in one commit. OpenKnowledge moves rewrite links in every file that points at the moved file, and this session's moves touched `bundles/`, `sources/`, and `research/` together. Such commits would need either splitting or an explicit, recorded maintenance exemption, which reintroduces self-report for that narrow case.

## Synthesis

Repository-held enforcement works at commit time, not write time, and it works through diff structure, not content state. The strongest single rule found is layer separation within a commit, which would have caught both observed near-misses deterministically and costs one extra commit per promotion. Augmentation guards and status-transition checks are useful additions against destructive or unearned changes. These are candidate checks, not installed enforcement. Wiring them into the installed pre-commit hook would cover commits from any harness in this clone; hosted CI would cover skipped or missing hooks only if the same checks were also added to `mise run ci`. Governance subsequently chose to report layer-separation violations without blocking work, as a measured signal; the other candidates remain undecided.[^ci][^governance]

The repository cannot verify intent or human verification. Those remain operator judgments, which the structural rules route to the operator by making the promotion a separate, reviewable commit.

## Open questions

- Is layer separation too blunt for link-rewriting moves, and is a recorded maintenance exemption acceptable given it relies on self-report?
- Should the validator gain a diff mode (against `HEAD` for pre-commit, against the merge base in CI), or should diff checks be a separate script?
- Should `sources/` and `research/` be treated as one side of the separation, or should `sources/`-to-`research/` changes also be split?
- Does the hook's clone-local scope matter for the operator's other machines, or is hosted CI enough?

## Promotion candidates

If accepted: layer separation within a commit, augmentation guards, and status-transition checks as candidate validator rules; and, for the governance draft, the finding that enforcement happens at commit time through diff structure. None is applied here.

# Research brief: a repository-held personal-computing agent

## Purpose and standing

This brief bounds research into building `src/personal_computing_agent` in this repository. It records the idea, the risk that keeps it honest, the design frame taken from the reference implementations, and the questions research must answer before any code. It decides nothing.

## Origin

The write-boundary research concluded that BB cannot gate writes by path and that the repository must carry the guarantee, at commit time, through diff structure.[^bb-pass][^repo-pass] The operator then asked why not build a repository-held agent, as both main references do: the OKF reference agent and OpenWiki are each a repo-held program that owns the path from sources to knowledge.[^operator][^ref-agent][^ow-research]

## The named risk (backpressure)

The operator's Project Learning Framework compiled structure where none existed and worked, but it fell into the classic trap of the compiler: it exists to serve itself.[^arc] VIO-0002 records the same failure for architecture promoted into hard rules before use justified them.[^vio-0002] An agent built before the rules it automates are decided would repeat both.

This risk is recorded as standing backpressure on the research and on any build that follows it:

- Every command the package exposes must answer to a governance rule that has been decided. A command that cannot name its rule is not built.
- Nothing that automates an undecided rule is built. Undecided rules stay in research until governance decides them.
- The package is judged by whether it serves the registry's purpose, not by its own completeness.

The operator named this risk as what keeps the work honest.[^operator]

## Design frame: responsibility layers in code

OpenWiki's coding-agent integration supplies the frame. Every host gets one canonical skill and the same five MCP tools (`openwiki_begin`, `openwiki_submit_plan`, `openwiki_next_page`, `openwiki_submit_page`, `openwiki_finish`). The host model researches and authors only the current page job; OpenWiki owns durable run state, Claims reconciliation, finalization, metadata, provenance, and managed setup files. Host differences live in one registry of install paths and config formats, with unsupported scopes recorded as unsupported rather than guessed. The v1 boundary is kept deliberately narrow.[^ow-contrib] The OKF reference agent has the same shape: its runner hands out one concept per run and `write_concept_doc` is the guarded write path.[^ref-agent]

The operator identified this as the main lesson: it is the operator's responsibility layers expressed in code.[^operator] The tool is the project-level manager: it owns the queue, the definition of each unit, validation at submission, and the decision that work is complete. The harness is the bounded work unit: it investigates and authors one unit and never declares the run done. This matches the confirmed mapping of domain management, project, and bounded work.[^workshop]

This corrects an earlier framing of "a tool first, an agent later, or never." The agent is always present, as whichever harness does the work. The design question is the contract between the lifecycle owner and the worker, not whether an agent exists.

It also adds a checkpoint earlier than the commit. Work that goes through the protocol is validated at submission and cannot finish until state is valid; the proposed commit-time layer-separation check reports violations without blocking work, including work outside the protocol. It supplies the measured signal chosen in governance; it is not a blocking backstop.[^repo-pass][^governance]

## Maintainer and consumer boundary

OpenWiki's own `AGENTS.md` is written for an agent maintaining OpenWiki: it treats OpenWiki's source code and tests as authoritative and its generated wiki as an optional evidence index, and asks agents not to hand-edit generated pages but to change sources and let OpenWiki regenerate. ## Important disclaimer

This record captures what I noticed right after two research passes on branch `feat/governance-application`. An agent drafted it from my statements and from what happened in the session; I have not reviewed it line by line. It rests on one session and one sequence of events. It is not a finding that the split works in general, and it is not an assessment of the agent.

## Positive observations

What naturally fell out: we created the governance draft, almost kept writing to it, then backed off and wrote research based on the reference examples instead. Five questions fell out as friction. To me that means the split works.

Each kind of material landed in its own layer. The three reference implementations (the OKF reference agent, OpenKnowledge, and OpenWiki) became cited sources. The synthesis became two draft research documents, [OKF plugin scope](../../research/2026-10-04-okf-plugin-scope-and-source-status.md) and [OpenWiki claims and source trust](../../research/2026-10-05-openwiki-claims-and-source-trust.md), each ending in promotion candidates with none applied. The friction became five open questions. The [governance draft](../../bundles/_repo/governance.md) stayed unchanged because nothing had been decided.

The research passes cite each other through their sources rather than through governance, so the evidence chain exists without touching knowledge.

## Open questions

- Would the boundary have held without me redirecting it?
- Do the five questions read differently because they arrived as research friction rather than as edits to governance?
- Is one session enough to say the split works, or only that it can work?

## Negative or surprising observation

The boundary held because I held it, not because anything enforced it. The agent reached for the governance draft twice: first to answer the OKF plugin scoping question directly in its open points, then to add a pointer from governance to the new research. Both times I redirected it, the first time by saying this was a research pass. Nothing in the repository would have refused either edit.

## Experienced pattern

1. The governance draft existed and had open points.
2. A reference implementation answered one of those open points.
3. The agent proposed writing the answer into governance.
4. Inflection point: I named it a research pass, not a governance change.
5. Findings went to `research/` as a draft with promotion candidates; governance stayed unchanged.
6. The same move repeated with OpenWiki, and five open questions fell out of the two passes as friction.

The governance draft remains a record of decided things only. The undecided material is collected in two research documents and five questions that can be taken up one at a time, rather than being settled implicitly by the last edit. My attention was needed twice to keep it that way.

These are questions for later review, not conclusions.

## Next review, if pursued

Compare this record against the two research documents, the unchanged governance draft, the commit history of `feat/governance-application`, and the session in which both redirections happened. Preserve the distinction between what happened, what I concluded about the split, and what the agent's behavior shows about default write targets.

# Repository-held enforcement of the knowledge write boundary

## Purpose and standing

This is Pass 2 of the [write-boundary research brief](2026-10-05-write-boundary-enforcement-brief.md), scoped by [Pass 1](2026-10-05-bb-write-boundary-pass.md), which ruled out BB as the enforcement point and concluded that the repository must carry the guarantee.[^brief][^bb-pass] The question here is how early and how precisely repository-held code can enforce the boundary. It is provisional research; nothing here changes the validator, hooks, or governance.

## Correction to the brief

The brief stated that the pre-commit hook was not installed. That repeated an outdated gap. The scanning policy records that the hook was installed on 2026-09-05 for this clone, chaining Entire to hk, while installation in other clones or on other machines is not established.[^scanning] The installed `pre-commit` hook runs `hk run pre-commit` through mise, and the hook ran on every commit in this session.[^hooks] It runs whitespace, newline, merge-conflict, private-key, and staged-secret checks; it does not run the OKF validator.[^hk]

## Findings

### Q5. Which checks are deterministic from content, and which would have caught the near-misses

The [observation](../sources/observations/2026-10-05-research-layer-held-the-boundary-observation-log.md) records two near-misses: answering the OKF plugin scoping question directly in the governance draft's open points, and adding a pointer from governance to new research.[^observation] Both are edits to a `draft` Policy that already carries `sources`.

Content-only checks read one file state at a time. Candidates include: every bundle concept carries `sources`; a `stable` concept carries a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor; a `draft` concept cites something in `sources/` or `research/`. The governance draft satisfies all of them before and after either near-miss. **No content-only check would have caught either near-miss**, because the problem was not the resulting state but the act of changing knowledge without a promotion.

Diff checks compare a change against its base, and several are deterministic:

- **Separation of layers within a commit.** A single commit may not change both `research/` (or `sources/`) and `bundles/`. Research and promotion become separate units. Both near-misses arose mid-research, so they would most likely have been committed alongside the research they came from (an inference; neither was written). In that case this rule catches both without trusting anything the agent says.
- **Augmentation guards.** Adapted from the OKF reference agent's write guards: an existing bundle concept may not lose `sources` entries or top-level headings.[^ref-agent] These protect against destructive rewrites; they would not catch either near-miss, which only added text.
- **Status transitions.** A concept moving to `stable` must add a new `verified` entry in the same change.

### Q6. How close to write time repository-held code can act

Repository code cannot see a write as it happens; Pass 1 showed no harness-agnostic write-time gate exists.[^bb-pass] The earliest repository-held point every harness and every manual edit reaches is the commit, through the installed pre-commit hook. Adding a validator step there runs the boundary checks for all four harnesses at once. Two limits apply: hooks are clone-local and can be skipped with `--no-verify`. Hosted CI runs `mise run ci` on pull requests and pushes to `main`, but that task does not currently run any of these candidate diff checks. CI could check the same diff only after that validator is wired into the shared task graph. For layer separation, governance has since chosen reporting violations without blocking work; neither hook nor CI would make that signal a rejecting gate.[^ci][^governance]

The commit is also the unit of review in this repository, so enforcement there matches how work is accepted. In both near-misses the proposed change had not yet been written, so nothing at any layer would have fired; the operator's redirection happened at proposal time, which no tool reaches.

### Q7. Telling a promotion from an ordinary edit without trusting the agent

Some structure is visible without self-report: which layers a commit touches, whether `sources` or headings shrank, whether a status moved. Intent is not. Any marker that says "this is a promotion" or "this is maintenance", such as a commit trailer, is written by whoever commits, agent or human. Likewise, a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor proves only that someone wrote one; the repository cannot authenticate that a person verified anything. The structural rules above avoid this by constraining shape rather than reading intent.

### Q8. Cost to legitimate work

The layer-separation rule costs one extra commit per promotion: research lands first, the promotion lands separately and cites it. That matches the governance draft's model, in which a promotion pass is a deliberate step after research.[^governance] Its real cost is mechanical maintenance that crosses layers in one commit. OpenKnowledge moves rewrite links in every file that points at the moved file, and this session's moves touched `bundles/`, `sources/`, and `research/` together. Such commits would need either splitting or an explicit, recorded maintenance exemption, which reintroduces self-report for that narrow case.

## Synthesis

Repository-held enforcement works at commit time, not write time, and it works through diff structure, not content state. The strongest single rule found is layer separation within a commit, which would have caught both observed near-misses deterministically and costs one extra commit per promotion. Augmentation guards and status-transition checks are useful additions against destructive or unearned changes. These are candidate checks, not installed enforcement. Wiring them into the installed pre-commit hook would cover commits from any harness in this clone; hosted CI would cover skipped or missing hooks only if the same checks were also added to `mise run ci`. Governance subsequently chose to report layer-separation violations without blocking work, as a measured signal; the other candidates remain undecided.[^ci][^governance]

The repository cannot verify intent or human verification. Those remain operator judgments, which the structural rules route to the operator by making the promotion a separate, reviewable commit.

## Open questions

- Is layer separation too blunt for link-rewriting moves, and is a recorded maintenance exemption acceptable given it relies on self-report?
- Should the validator gain a diff mode (against `HEAD` for pre-commit, against the merge base in CI), or should diff checks be a separate script?
- Should `sources/` and `research/` be treated as one side of the separation, or should `sources/`-to-`research/` changes also be split?
- Does the hook's clone-local scope matter for the operator's other machines, or is hosted CI enough?

## Promotion candidates

If accepted: layer separation within a commit, augmentation guards, and status-transition checks as candidate validator rules; and, for the governance draft, the finding that enforcement happens at commit time through diff structure. None is applied here.

# Observation Log: The Research Layer Held the Boundary

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Project | personal-computing (3I lab) |
| Captured | 2026-10-05 |
| Observation period | 2026-10-04 late evening through 2026-10-05 early morning |
| Subject | First use of the sources / research / knowledge split on governance work |
| Record type | Operator observation and preliminary assessment, drafted by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) from the operator's statements and the session record |
| Status | Captured while fresh; not yet validated |

## Important disclaimer

This record captures what I noticed right after two research passes on branch `feat/governance-application`. An agent drafted it from my statements and from what happened in the session; I have not reviewed it line by line. It rests on one session and one sequence of events. It is not a finding that the split works in general, and it is not an assessment of the agent.

## Positive observations

What naturally fell out: we created the governance draft, almost kept writing to it, then backed off and wrote research based on the reference examples instead. Five questions fell out as friction. To me that means the split works.

Each kind of material landed in its own layer. The three reference implementations (the OKF reference agent, OpenKnowledge, and OpenWiki) became cited sources. The synthesis became two draft research documents, [OKF plugin scope](../../research/2026-10-04-okf-plugin-scope-and-source-status.md) and [OpenWiki claims and source trust](../../research/2026-10-05-openwiki-claims-and-source-trust.md), each ending in promotion candidates with none applied. The friction became five open questions. The [governance draft](../../bundles/_repo/governance.md) stayed unchanged because nothing had been decided.

The research passes cite each other through their sources rather than through governance, so the evidence chain exists without touching knowledge.

## Open questions

- Would the boundary have held without me redirecting it?
- Do the five questions read differently because they arrived as research friction rather than as edits to governance?
- Is one session enough to say the split works, or only that it can work?

## Negative or surprising observation

The boundary held because I held it, not because anything enforced it. The agent reached for the governance draft twice: first to answer the OKF plugin scoping question directly in its open points, then to add a pointer from governance to the new research. Both times I redirected it, the first time by saying this was a research pass. Nothing in the repository would have refused either edit.

## Experienced pattern

1. The governance draft existed and had open points.
2. A reference implementation answered one of those open points.
3. The agent proposed writing the answer into governance.
4. Inflection point: I named it a research pass, not a governance change.
5. Findings went to `research/` as a draft with promotion candidates; governance stayed unchanged.
6. The same move repeated with OpenWiki, and five open questions fell out of the two passes as friction.

## Impact

The governance draft remains a record of decided things only. The undecided material is collected in two research documents and five questions that can be taken up one at a time, rather than being settled implicitly by the last edit. My attention was needed twice to keep it that way.

## Preliminary assessment

Working hypotheses, plausible and not mutually exclusive:

- **The split works when it is named.** Calling the work a research pass was enough to route it correctly; having `research/` as a real place to put it made the redirection cheap.
- **The boundary depends on operator attention.** The agent's default was to write where the open point lived. Without a refusal mechanism, the boundary is as strong as the operator's vigilance in the moment. This matches the write-boundary finding in the OpenWiki research, where tooling, not the agent, owns what may be written.

## Gap highlighted

- What would make a write to `bundles/` from a research activity refuse or warn without relying on the operator?
- How should an agent recognize that an answer to an open governance point is research, not a governance edit?
- Is "which writes a promotion pass should be refused" the first of the five questions to take up, given this record?

These are questions for later review, not conclusions.

## Next review, if pursued

Compare this record against the two research documents, the unchanged governance draft, the commit history of `feat/governance-application`, and the session in which both redirections happened. Preserve the distinction between what happened, what I concluded about the split, and what the agent's behavior shows about default write targets.

# Repository-held enforcement of the knowledge write boundary

## Purpose and standing

This is Pass 2 of the [write-boundary research brief](2026-10-05-write-boundary-enforcement-brief.md), scoped by [Pass 1](2026-10-05-bb-write-boundary-pass.md), which ruled out BB as the enforcement point and concluded that the repository must carry the guarantee.[^brief][^bb-pass] The question here is how early and how precisely repository-held code can enforce the boundary. It is provisional research; nothing here changes the validator, hooks, or governance.

## Correction to the brief

The brief stated that the pre-commit hook was not installed. That repeated an outdated gap. The scanning policy records that the hook was installed on 2026-09-05 for this clone, chaining Entire to hk, while installation in other clones or on other machines is not established.[^scanning] The installed `pre-commit` hook runs `hk run pre-commit` through mise, and the hook ran on every commit in this session.[^hooks] It runs whitespace, newline, merge-conflict, private-key, and staged-secret checks; it does not run the OKF validator.[^hk]

## Findings

### Q5. Which checks are deterministic from content, and which would have caught the near-misses

The [observation](../sources/observations/2026-10-05-research-layer-held-the-boundary-observation-log.md) records two near-misses: answering the OKF plugin scoping question directly in the governance draft's open points, and adding a pointer from governance to new research.[^observation] Both are edits to a `draft` Policy that already carries `sources`.

Content-only checks read one file state at a time. Candidates include: every bundle concept carries `sources`; a `stable` concept carries a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor; a `draft` concept cites something in `sources/` or `research/`. The governance draft satisfies all of them before and after either near-miss. **No content-only check would have caught either near-miss**, because the problem was not the resulting state but the act of changing knowledge without a promotion.

Diff checks compare a change against its base, and several are deterministic:

- **Separation of layers within a commit.** A single commit may not change both `research/` (or `sources/`) and `bundles/`. Research and promotion become separate units. Both near-misses arose mid-research, so they would most likely have been committed alongside the research they came from (an inference; neither was written). In that case this rule catches both without trusting anything the agent says.
- **Augmentation guards.** Adapted from the OKF reference agent's write guards: an existing bundle concept may not lose `sources` entries or top-level headings.[^ref-agent] These protect against destructive rewrites; they would not catch either near-miss, which only added text.
- **Status transitions.** A concept moving to `stable` must add a new `verified` entry in the same change.

### Q6. How close to write time repository-held code can act

Repository code cannot see a write as it happens; Pass 1 showed no harness-agnostic write-time gate exists.[^bb-pass] The earliest repository-held point every harness and every manual edit reaches is the commit, through the installed pre-commit hook. Adding a validator step there runs the boundary checks for all four harnesses at once. Two limits apply: hooks are clone-local and can be skipped with `--no-verify`. Hosted CI runs `mise run ci` on pull requests and pushes to `main`, but that task does not currently run any of these candidate diff checks. CI could check the same diff only after that validator is wired into the shared task graph. For layer separation, governance has since chosen reporting violations without blocking work; neither hook nor CI would make that signal a rejecting gate.[^ci][^governance]

The commit is also the unit of review in this repository, so enforcement there matches how work is accepted. In both near-misses the proposed change had not yet been written, so nothing at any layer would have fired; the operator's redirection happened at proposal time, which no tool reaches.

### Q7. Telling a promotion from an ordinary edit without trusting the agent

Some structure is visible without self-report: which layers a commit touches, whether `sources` or headings shrank, whether a status moved. Intent is not. Any marker that says "this is a promotion" or "this is maintenance", such as a commit trailer, is written by whoever commits, agent or human. Likewise, a `verified` entry with a `human:` actor proves only that someone wrote one; the repository cannot authenticate that a person verified anything. The structural rules above avoid this by constraining shape rather than reading intent.

### Q8. Cost to legitimate work

The layer-separation rule costs one extra commit per promotion: research lands first, the promotion lands separately and cites it. That matches the governance draft's model, in which a promotion pass is a deliberate step after research.[^governance] Its real cost is mechanical maintenance that crosses layers in one commit. OpenKnowledge moves rewrite links in every file that points at the moved file, and this session's moves touched `bundles/`, `sources/`, and `research/` together. Such commits would need either splitting or an explicit, recorded maintenance exemption, which reintroduces self-report for that narrow case.

## Synthesis

Repository-held enforcement works at commit time, not write time, and it works through diff structure, not content state. The strongest single rule found is layer separation within a commit, which would have caught both observed near-misses deterministically and costs one extra commit per promotion. Augmentation guards and status-transition checks are useful additions against destructive or unearned changes. These are candidate checks, not installed enforcement. Wiring them into the installed pre-commit hook would cover commits from any harness in this clone; hosted CI would cover skipped or missing hooks only if the same checks were also added to `mise run ci`. Governance subsequently chose to report layer-separation violations without blocking work, as a measured signal; the other candidates remain undecided.[^ci][^governance]

The repository cannot verify intent or human verification. Those remain operator judgments, which the structural rules route to the operator by making the promotion a separate, reviewable commit.

## Open questions

- Is layer separation too blunt for link-rewriting moves, and is a recorded maintenance exemption acceptable given it relies on self-report?
- Should the validator gain a diff mode (against `HEAD` for pre-commit, against the merge base in CI), or should diff checks be a separate script?
- Should `sources/` and `research/` be treated as one side of the separation, or should `sources/`-to-`research/` changes also be split?
- Does the hook's clone-local scope matter for the operator's other machines, or is hosted CI enough?

## Promotion candidates

If accepted: layer separation within a commit, augmentation guards, and status-transition checks as candidate validator rules; and, for the governance draft, the finding that enforcement happens at commit time through diff structure. None is applied here.
